value.name: Container environment model
value.expression: Application + configuration + libraries + dependencies -> container -> isolated processes
value.meaning: Source describes containers as environments surrounding applications and bundling related software dependencies while isolating processes.

value.name: Shared kernel model
value.expression: Container_1 + Container_2 + ... + Container_n -> common OS kernel
value.meaning: Multiple containers collectively share a common operating-system kernel.

value.name: Container portability model
value.expression: Bundled application environment + compatible runtime -> cloud/non-cloud deployment across vendors
value.meaning: Containerization is framed as allowing applications to run across cloud or non-cloud environments regardless of vendor.

value.name: OCI interoperability model
value.expression: Standard image + standard runtime + standard distribution -> interoperability across implementations/tools
value.meaning: OCI specifications are intended to make images and runtimes interoperable across implementations and tools.

value.name: Container runtime lifecycle
value.expression: Runtime configuration -> execution environment -> container lifecycle
value.meaning: OCI Runtime Specification defines configuration, execution environment and lifecycle.

value.name: Container image structure
value.expression: Image = manifest + filesystem layers + configuration
value.meaning: OCI Image Specification defines these image components.

value.name: Container cluster management
value.expression: Cluster management = create + upgrade + repair + balance + scale + log + monitor
value.meaning: Source lists these as cluster management functions.

value.name: Demand-responsive scaling
value.expression: User demand change -> start/stop instances -> adjusted capacity
value.meaning: Cluster management adapts capacity to number of users by starting or stopping instances.

value.name: Shared-kernel security boundary
value.expression: Shared OS kernel -> common attack surface -> possible system-wide impact
value.meaning: Source warns that shared OS architecture can allow security threats to affect the whole containerized system.

value.name: Container orchestration
value.expression: Application containers + orchestration controller -> coordinated container management
value.meaning: Orchestration is mainly used for application containers and includes Kubernetes and Docker Swarm.

value.event: Containerization became widely adopted by major cloud platforms.
The U.S. Department of Defense pursued containerization for faster software development and fielding, with first application in the F-22.
OCI maintains Runtime, Image and Distribution specifications for container interoperability.

value.name: Container vs Virtual Machine
value.description: Containerization uses OS/application-level virtualization and shared kernels; system VMs can provide whole-machine/guest-OS abstractions.

value.name: OS Container vs Application Container
value.description: Source identifies OS containers and application containers as distinct container types.

value.name: Container vs Container Image
value.description: Container is an execution environment; image is a packaged artifact whose structure is standardized by OCI.

value.name: Image vs Runtime
value.description: Image describes packaged filesystem/configuration content; runtime defines execution environment and lifecycle.

value.name: Runtime Specification vs Image Specification
value.description: Runtime Specification covers execution/lifecycle; Image Specification covers image structure.

value.name: OCI Distribution vs Image Specification
value.description: Distribution concerns image distribution; Image Specification concerns image representation.

value.name: Container Management vs Orchestration
value.description: Management encompasses operational functions; orchestration specifically coordinates application containers.

value.name: Orchestration vs Cluster Management
value.description: Orchestration coordinates application containers; cluster management covers infrastructure/cluster lifecycle, scaling and observability.

value.name: Shared Kernel vs Separate Guest OS
value.description: Containers share a kernel; system VMs provide guest OS execution.

value.name: Portability vs Interoperability
value.description: Portability concerns running across environments/vendors; interoperability concerns compatible implementations/tools under common standards.

value.name: OS Security Scanning vs Application Security
value.description: Protecting the host OS does not necessarily protect application containers.

value.name: Scaling vs Load Balancing
value.description: Scaling changes the number of instances; load balancing distributes load among existing instances.

value.name: Logging vs Monitoring
value.description: Logging records activities; monitoring observes logs, applications or sensors.

value.name: Container Runtime vs Container Manager
value.description: Runtime implements execution/lifecycle; manager/orchestrator manages groups/workloads.

value.name: Cloud vs Non-cloud Container Deployment
value.description: Containerization explicitly spans both cloud and non-cloud environments.

value.name: Container Security Benefit vs Security Risk
value.description: Isolation provides separation, but shared-kernel architecture creates a broader security concern.

value.name: Cluster Repair vs Upgrade
value.description: Repair restores operational state; upgrade changes software versions/state.

value.name: Application Dependency vs Kernel Dependency
value.description: Libraries/configuration/dependencies are bundled per application; containers still depend on a shared OS kernel.

value.misconception: Containers are just small virtual machines.
value.correction: The source frames containers as OS/application-level virtualization and emphasizes shared kernel operation.

value.misconception: Every container has its own operating-system kernel.
value.correction: Multiple containers collectively share a common OS kernel.

value.misconception: A container is the same thing as a container image.
value.correction: The image is the packaged artifact; the container is the execution environment.

value.misconception: OCI only standardizes container images.
value.correction: OCI maintains Runtime, Image and Distribution specifications.

value.misconception: OCI Runtime Specification defines image layers.
value.correction: Runtime Specification defines configuration/execution/lifecycle; image layers belong to Image Specification.

value.misconception: Orchestration and cluster management are identical.
value.correction: The source distinguishes application-container orchestration from broader cluster management functions.

value.misconception: Scaling just means load balancing.
value.correction: Scaling changes instance count; load balancing balances work among existing instances.

value.misconception: OS security scanning automatically secures application containers.
value.correction: The source explicitly warns that scanners generally protect the OS but may not protect application containers.

value.misconception: Containerization only applies to public cloud.
value.correction: The source explicitly includes non-cloud environments.

value.misconception: Containerization eliminates security risk through isolation.
value.correction: The shared OS can allow security threats to affect the whole containerized system.

value.misconception: Kubernetes is the only container orchestrator.
value.correction: The source names both Kubernetes and Docker Swarm and its taxonomy also lists OpenShift and Amazon ECS.

value.misconception: Container clusters only need scheduling.
value.correction: The source lists creation, upgrades, repair, balancing, scaling, logging and monitoring.

source_claims.claim: Containerization is OS-level or application-level virtualization enabling isolated user spaces across cloud or non-cloud environments.
Containers surround applications, bundle configuration/libraries/dependencies, isolate processes, and collectively share an OS kernel.
Containerization is widely adopted by major cloud platforms and pursued by the U.S. Department of Defense, first applied to the F-22.
Shared OS architecture creates security concerns and OS-focused scanning may leave application containers insufficiently protected.
OCI develops Runtime, Image and Distribution specifications intended to provide interoperability.
Container orchestration/management is mainly used for application containers, with Kubernetes and Docker Swarm named as implementations.
Container cluster management includes creation, upgrade, repair, load balancing, scaling, logging and monitoring.
The source provides journal literature covering containerization technologies, applications, challenges and cloud distributed systems.
The source provides books on containerization and Docker.
The source provides additional references including Kubernetes, Red Hat, IBM, OCI and orchestration resources.

value.distinction: C++ vs C

value.distinction: Language vs implementation
value.explanation: C++ is the standardized language; GCC/Clang/MSVC/etc. are implementations.

value.distinction: Standard vs Core Guidelines
value.explanation: ISO defines the language/library; Core Guidelines are external guidance.

value.distinction: Header vs module
value.explanation: Headers are traditional inclusion; modules provide importable/named mechanisms.

value.distinction: Inline vs standalone assembly
value.explanation: Inline is compiler-specific embedded assembly; standalone is separate and linked.

value.distinction: Source vs object code
value.explanation: Source is program text; object code is compiled binary output.

value.distinction: Source compatibility vs ABI compatibility
value.explanation: Similar source does not guarantee binary compatibility across compilers.

value.distinction: Templates vs virtual dispatch
value.explanation: Templates provide generic programming; virtual functions provide dynamic dispatch.

value.distinction: C linkage vs C++ linkage
value.explanation: extern C selects C linkage for interoperating functions.

value.distinction: STL vs standard library
value.explanation: STL's core generic model is part of a larger standard library.

value.distinction: Manual control vs safety
value.explanation: Manual memory is a capability whose misuse can create risks.

value.distinction: Standard revision vs compiler version
value.explanation: C++23/C++26 are language revisions, not compiler names.

source_claims.statement: C++ originated as an extension of C and evolved into a multi-paradigm language.
Stroustrup began C with Classes at Bell Labs in 1979.
C++ combines direct hardware mapping with zero-overhead abstractions.
C++ is standardized by ISO WG21 and has successive revisions.
The standard library spans containers, iterators, ranges, algorithms, numerics, I/O, memory, metaprogramming, diagnostics and concurrency.
The STL model of containers, iterators and generic algorithms became part of the standard library.
C++ is not strictly a superset of C.
extern C enables C linkage for mixed C/C++ functions.
Assembly integration varies by compiler and architecture.
Core Guidelines target type/resource safety but are not ISO consensus.
Manual memory misuse can introduce security risks such as buffer overflow.
C++ influenced a broad set of later languages.

value.name: Cryptographic hash function
value.definition: A deterministic algorithm that maps an arbitrary-length binary input to a fixed-length digest, with security goals including preimage resistance, second-preimage resistance, and collision resistance.

value.primary_source: User-supplied Wikipedia article text: Cryptographic hash function
value.scope_note: The graph follows the supplied article's terminology and coverage, while adding explicit relationship structure, schema, patterns, and cautious engineering rules for machine use.
source_derived_content: Merkle–Damgård, wide-pipe, sponge, and HAIFA constructions
value.editorial_caveat: Algorithm status and parameter recommendations change. Use current standards and expert review for production decisions; the graph is not a substitute for a cryptographic design review.

value.name: Secure file verification
value.purpose: Detect modification or substitution of downloaded content.
steps: Obtain the expected digest from an authenticated/trusted source.
Compute the digest of the received file with a suitable modern algorithm.
Compare values using the correct algorithm and encoding.
If a mismatch occurs, reject or investigate the file; if it matches, interpret the result only within the trust model.
caveats: A digest posted beside a file on the same unauthenticated channel may be replaced together with the file.
A matching hash does not prove that software is benign or that the publisher is trustworthy.

value.name: Password storage with a password KDF
value.purpose: Reduce the rate of offline password guessing after a verifier database is exposed.
steps: Generate a unique random salt per password.
Derive a verifier using a password KDF such as Argon2, scrypt, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with appropriate parameters.
Store the algorithm identifier, parameters, salt, and verifier.
On login, recompute and compare; upgrade parameters as policy changes.
caveats: Do not store plaintext passwords.
Do not use a fast hash such as raw SHA-256 or SHA-1 alone for password storage.
Parameter choices should follow current platform and standards guidance.

value.name: HMAC message authentication
value.purpose: Authenticate messages using a shared secret and a standardized keyed construction.
steps: Agree on a secure hash and shared secret key.
Compute the HMAC over the canonical message representation.
Transmit the message and authentication tag.
Receiver recomputes the HMAC and compares tags using an appropriate constant-time comparison.
caveats: Do not substitute naive hash(secret || message) constructions for HMAC.
Key management and message canonicalization remain important.

value.name: Content-addressed storage
value.purpose: Address and deduplicate objects based on content.
steps: Select a collision-resistant hash and a canonical byte representation.
Hash the content to derive a content address.
Store the object and index its address to physical storage.
On retrieval, recompute the hash to verify content integrity.
caveats: Collision handling and algorithm migration should be part of the design.
The content address is not automatically a claim of publisher authenticity.

value.name: Merkle-tree verification
value.purpose: Commit to a large data set and verify components using a root digest and authentication path.
steps: Hash each leaf using an unambiguous encoding.
Hash internal nodes from their child hashes.
Publish or authenticate the root digest.
Verify a selected leaf by recomputing its path to the root.
caveats: Tree layout, leaf/node domain separation, and encoding must be specified to avoid ambiguity.

value.name: Hash-based proof of work
value.purpose: Make request creation moderately costly while allowing cheap validation.
steps: Define a target predicate over a hash output.
Vary a nonce or candidate header and compute hashes until the predicate passes.
Send the candidate and proof.
Verifier performs one or a small number of hash computations and checks the predicate.
caveats: Difficulty must be calibrated; proof of work does not itself establish the truth or legitimacy of the submitted content.

value.name: Cryptographic hash algorithm migration
value.purpose: Retire weak digest algorithms while maintaining interoperability.
steps: Inventory every algorithm use and stored identifier format.
Choose a modern algorithm appropriate to the use case and threat model.
Version formats and APIs so algorithm identity is explicit.
Where feasible, verify old objects and add new digests; plan dual-read or staged migration.
Monitor standards and cryptanalysis and retire obsolete formats.
caveats: A digest's byte length alone does not uniquely identify the algorithm.
Do not assume legacy digests become secure because they are combined with a modern digest.

value.statement: A cryptographic hash is not encryption and has no decryption key or general inverse operation.
A matching digest proves only a content match relative to the expected digest and trust chain; it does not establish that the content is safe or benign.
For an ideal n-bit hash, generic preimage work is about 2^n and generic collision work about 2^(n/2); real algorithms may be weaker due to cryptanalysis.
Fast general-purpose hashes should not be used alone to store passwords; use a salted password KDF with current recommended parameters.
For hash-based message authentication, use HMAC or another reviewed construction rather than naive secret-prefix/suffix hashing.
MD5 and SHA-1 are unsuitable for new applications that depend on collision resistance.
CRC-32 and similar checksums detect accidental corruption but do not provide cryptographic protection against intentional manipulation.
Persist the algorithm name/version and output parameters alongside a digest; digest bytes alone are not a robust self-describing identifier.

value.title: File digest comparison
value.input: A downloaded archive and a trusted SHA-256 digest string.
steps: Compute SHA-256 over the exact downloaded bytes.
Encode the result consistently, commonly as hexadecimal.
Compare with the authenticated expected digest.
value.output: Equal digests provide strong evidence of byte-for-byte identity under SHA-256's security assumptions and the trust model.

value.title: Leading-zero proof of work
value.input: A candidate message/header plus a nonce.
steps: Hash the candidate.
Check whether the digest begins with the required number of zero bits.
If not, vary the nonce and repeat.
value.output: A valid candidate is relatively cheap to verify; expected search effort grows exponentially with the number of required leading zero bits.

value.title: Digest commitment
value.input: A secret solution m held by Alice.
steps: Alice computes H(m) and publishes the digest before revealing m.
Bob later computes H(m) over the revealed solution.
They compare the result to the earlier commitment.
value.output: The matching digest supports the claim that the revealed solution matches the committed value, assuming the hash and protocol are appropriate.

value.title: Salted password verifier
value.input: Password candidate, unique random salt, KDF name and parameters.
steps: Derive a verifier with the selected password KDF.
Store the salt, algorithm parameters and verifier, not the plaintext password.
At login, derive again and compare.
value.output: Unique salts reduce cross-account precomputation and KDF cost slows each password guess.

value.name: CSS rule structure
value.expression: stylesheet → rule → selector(s) + declaration block → property:value
value.mechanism: Selectors determine targets; declarations assign values.

value.name: Cascade resolution
value.expression: matching declarations → priority/importance → specificity → source order → selected value
value.mechanism: The cascade resolves competing declarations using priority and tie-break rules.

value.name: Selector matching
value.expression: selector + DOM structure/attributes/state → matching elements
value.mechanism: Selectors can use element type, IDs, classes, attributes, relationships, pseudo-classes, and pseudo-elements.

value.name: Inheritance
value.expression: ancestor value → eligible descendant property
value.mechanism: Some properties inherit from ancestors when not overridden.

value.name: Box model
value.expression: content + padding + border + margin → box geometry
value.mechanism: Element dimensions and surrounding spacing determine layout geometry.

value.name: External stylesheet reuse
value.expression: HTML → link stylesheet → shared CSS → rules applied across pages
value.mechanism: A common stylesheet reduces repetition and can be cached.

value.name: Responsive presentation
value.expression: viewport/device/media → media query → selected rules → adapted layout
value.mechanism: Conditional styling changes presentation across screens, orientations, and output media.

value.name: Browser compatibility workflow
value.expression: feature → support data → cross-browser test → @supports/fallback → resilient output
value.mechanism: Compatibility information and fallbacks reduce browser-specific failures.

value.name: Preprocessor compilation
value.expression: Sass/Less/Stylus source → compiler → CSS → browser rendering
value.mechanism: Preprocessors provide authoring abstractions but the browser receives CSS.

value.name: Multi-medium presentation
value.expression: semantic markup → user/media-specific styles → screen/print/speech/Braille output
value.mechanism: Separation permits the same content to be presented in different forms.

value.name: Framework styling
value.expression: framework stylesheet → reusable patterns → page layout
value.mechanism: Frameworks accelerate common design tasks but may introduce unused CSS overhead.

value.name: Presentational markup migration
value.expression: repeated HTML formatting → shared CSS rules → simpler markup
value.mechanism: Moving style declarations out of markup reduces duplication and maintenance effort.

value.distinction: HTML defines structure/content; CSS defines presentation.
CSS controls styling/layout; JavaScript supplies behavior.
Selectors choose targets; declarations set property values.
Pseudo-classes describe state/context; pseudo-elements target generated or partial content.
An ID identifies a single document element; classes can be reused.
Cascade resolves competing declarations; inheritance passes eligible values from ancestors.
Specificity compares selector weights; source order is a tie-breaker.
Inline declarations attach to one element; external CSS centralizes reusable rules.
Absolute units use fixed reference measures; relative units depend on context.
Responsive styles adapt to viewport/device context.
CSS 3 is modular; the source rejects a single monolithic CSS 4 release.
Sass, Less, and Stylus add authoring abstractions and compile to CSS.
Frameworks speed development but can add unused features and overhead.
Prefixes historically targeted browser-specific behavior; @supports tests support conditions.
Separating presentation lets the same content be adapted to different media.
Some style-reuse limitations can be addressed by languages compiling to CSS.

value.misconception: CSS defines document structure.
value.correction: HTML defines structure; CSS specifies presentation.

value.misconception: A CSS class is itself a CSS subsystem feature.
value.correction: The class attribute belongs to the markup model; CSS selectors match its value.

value.misconception: Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements are identical.
value.correction: Pseudo-classes match state/context; pseudo-elements target generated or partial content.

value.misconception: The last CSS rule always wins.
value.correction: Importance and specificity can take precedence over source order.

value.misconception: Specificity works like decimal arithmetic.
value.correction: Specificity components are compared as separate weights.

value.misconception: Every CSS property inherits automatically.
value.correction: Only properties that inherit by their rules receive ancestor values.

value.misconception: ID and class selectors are interchangeable.
value.correction: IDs identify a document element; classes can be reused.

value.misconception: CSS is only for screen visuals.
value.correction: CSS can tailor print and source-described speech/Braille contexts.

value.misconception: CSS 4 is one unified version after CSS 3.
value.correction: The source describes CSS 3 as modules rather than a monolithic CSS 4.

value.misconception: Vendor prefixes guarantee interoperability.
value.correction: Browser-specific prefixes do not eliminate testing or fallback needs.

value.misconception: Framework CSS is always smaller than handcrafted CSS.
value.correction: Frameworks may include unused styles and add download/maintenance overhead.

value.misconception: Preprocessors replace browser CSS.
value.correction: Sass, Less, and Stylus compile to CSS processed by browsers.

value.misconception: Inline styles are best for site-wide consistency.
value.correction: External stylesheets centralize reusable rules and can be cached.

value.misconception: Responsive design just shrinks content.
value.correction: Responsive styles adapt layout to device, viewport, and orientation.

value.misconception: JavaScript polyfills are native CSS.
value.correction: Polyfills are JavaScript code that may emulate unsupported Web behavior.

value.misconception: CSS has no limitations.
value.correction: The source lists scoping, rule naming/composition, hover-control, and text-targeting limitations.

formal_models.name: Preprocessor compilation
formal_models.expression: Sass/Less/Stylus source → compiler → CSS → browser rendering
formal_models.mechanism: Preprocessors provide authoring abstractions but the browser receives CSS.

formal_models.name: Multi-medium presentation
formal_models.expression: semantic markup → user/media-specific styles → screen/print/speech/Braille output
formal_models.mechanism: Separation permits the same content to be presented in different forms.

formal_models.name: Framework styling
formal_models.expression: framework stylesheet → reusable patterns → page layout
formal_models.mechanism: Frameworks accelerate common design tasks but may introduce unused CSS overhead.

formal_models.name: Presentational markup migration
formal_models.expression: repeated HTML formatting → shared CSS rules → simpler markup
formal_models.mechanism: Moving style declarations out of markup reduces duplication and maintenance effort.

source_claims.claim: CSS specifies presentation of markup documents and is a core Web technology alongside HTML and JavaScript.
CSS separates content/structure from presentation, enabling reuse, maintainability, caching, accessibility, and alternate media.
CSS rules pair selectors with declaration blocks containing property-value declarations.
Selectors match elements by type, ID, class, attributes, relationships, state, and partial/generated content.
The cascade resolves competing declarations using priority, specificity, order, inheritance, and defaults.
CSS controls layout, dimensions, spacing, borders, typography, responsive design, and visual effects.
CSS can provide distinct presentation for screen, print, speech, Braille, and mobile contexts.
CSS originated in 1990s style-sheet proposals and CSS Level 1 was released in December 1996.
CSS 3 is developed as separate modules and summarized in periodic snapshots.
Browser differences are addressed with testing, feature queries, support tables, and fallbacks.
The source describes limitations involving scope, pseudo-class control, rule naming/composition, and arbitrary text targeting.
The ecosystem includes preprocessors, frameworks, extensions, and organization methodologies.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: HTML defines structure/content; CSS defines presentation.
CSS controls styling/layout; JavaScript supplies behavior.
Selectors choose targets; declarations set property values.
Pseudo-classes describe state/context; pseudo-elements target generated or partial content.
An ID identifies a single document element; classes can be reused.
Cascade resolves competing declarations; inheritance passes eligible values from ancestors.
Specificity compares selector weights; source order is a tie-breaker.
Inline declarations attach to one element; external CSS centralizes reusable rules.
Absolute units use fixed reference measures; relative units depend on context.
Responsive styles adapt to viewport/device context.
CSS 3 is modular; the source rejects a single monolithic CSS 4 release.
Sass, Less, and Stylus add authoring abstractions and compile to CSS.
Frameworks speed development but can add unused features and overhead.
Prefixes historically targeted browser-specific behavior; @supports tests support conditions.
Separating presentation lets the same content be adapted to different media.
Some style-reuse limitations can be addressed by languages compiling to CSS.

misconceptions.misconception: CSS defines document structure.
misconceptions.correction: HTML defines structure; CSS specifies presentation.

misconceptions.misconception: A CSS class is itself a CSS subsystem feature.
misconceptions.correction: The class attribute belongs to the markup model; CSS selectors match its value.

misconceptions.misconception: Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements are identical.
misconceptions.correction: Pseudo-classes match state/context; pseudo-elements target generated or partial content.

misconceptions.misconception: The last CSS rule always wins.
misconceptions.correction: Importance and specificity can take precedence over source order.

misconceptions.misconception: Specificity works like decimal arithmetic.
misconceptions.correction: Specificity components are compared as separate weights.

misconceptions.misconception: Every CSS property inherits automatically.
misconceptions.correction: Only properties that inherit by their rules receive ancestor values.

misconceptions.misconception: ID and class selectors are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: IDs identify a document element; classes can be reused.

misconceptions.misconception: CSS is only for screen visuals.
misconceptions.correction: CSS can tailor print and source-described speech/Braille contexts.

misconceptions.misconception: CSS 4 is one unified version after CSS 3.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes CSS 3 as modules rather than a monolithic CSS 4.

misconceptions.misconception: Vendor prefixes guarantee interoperability.
misconceptions.correction: Browser-specific prefixes do not eliminate testing or fallback needs.

misconceptions.misconception: Framework CSS is always smaller than handcrafted CSS.
misconceptions.correction: Frameworks may include unused styles and add download/maintenance overhead.

misconceptions.misconception: Preprocessors replace browser CSS.
misconceptions.correction: Sass, Less, and Stylus compile to CSS processed by browsers.

misconceptions.misconception: Inline styles are best for site-wide consistency.
misconceptions.correction: External stylesheets centralize reusable rules and can be cached.

misconceptions.misconception: Responsive design just shrinks content.
misconceptions.correction: Responsive styles adapt layout to device, viewport, and orientation.

misconceptions.misconception: JavaScript polyfills are native CSS.
misconceptions.correction: Polyfills are JavaScript code that may emulate unsupported Web behavior.

misconceptions.misconception: CSS has no limitations.
misconceptions.correction: The source lists scoping, rule naming/composition, hover-control, and text-targeting limitations.
